title: Renewed US-Iran Hostilities Send Oil Prices Surging and Revive Stagflation Fears
summary: A fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran unravelled this week after President Trump declared the interim peace deal 'over' and threatened fresh strikes and a naval blockade, sending Brent crude up more than 5% and reigniting the same inflation shock that has dogged the Fed all year. The episode matters less as a one-week price spike than as proof that the April ceasefire never removed the underlying risk — it only paused it — leaving energy markets, shipping lanes and monetary policy all hostage to a conflict that can reignite with a single presidential statement.
context:
- The April 2026 US-Iran ceasefire had allowed oil to drift back toward pre-war levels and given the Fed room to consider rate cuts; this week's escalation reverses that relief almost overnight, showing how conditional the 'peace dividend' priced into markets actually was.

- The immediate trigger was a series of attacks on vessels in or near the Strait of Hormuz, prompting the US-led Joint Maritime Information Center to raise its threat assessment for the waterway to 'severe' — a chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of global oil supply normally transits, making even a partial disruption highly price-sensitive.

- The IEA had been forecasting an oil surplus later in 2026 on the back of rising non-OPEC supply; a renewed conflict threatens to upend that surplus forecast, which is significant because a surplus was one of the few disinflationary forces working in the Fed's favour this year.

- Because May and June inflation readings were already elevated partly due to the earlier phase of the same conflict, a second energy-price shock lands on an economy with little room to absorb it without reigniting the exact stagflation dynamic — soft jobs growth alongside sticky prices — that has made this year's Fed decisions unusually difficult.

- Markets responded by pricing in materially higher odds of a Fed rate hike rather than a cut, a reminder that geopolitical risk is now feeding directly into the interest-rate outlook: energy shocks that would once have been treated as transitory are instead reshaping the path of policy itself.

title: Fed Minutes Reveal Deep Split Over Rates, Pushing Any Cut Out to 2027
summary: Minutes from the Fed's June meeting, released this week, show a central bank sharply divided over where rates go next, with roughly half of the committee favouring at least one more hike this year and the median projection now showing no rate cut until the second quarter of 2027. The disclosure matters because it marks a formal retreat from the market's earlier assumption that a softening labour market would force the Fed's hand — instead, inflation risk is winning out over growth concerns inside the committee itself.
context:
- The split follows Kevin Warsh's decision at the June meeting to strip forward guidance from the Fed's post-meeting statement, a deliberate move to preserve flexibility — the minutes show that flexibility is now being used to keep a hike on the table rather than to signal reassurance to markets.

- Nine of the eighteen FOMC participants indicated support for at least one hike this year, an unusually large hawkish bloc for a Fed that, as recently as the first quarter of 2026, was widely expected to be cutting by now.

- Pushing the first projected cut out to Q2 2027 represents a significant repricing from where market expectations sat just months ago, when soft jobs data had investors betting on relief as early as this autumn.

- The minutes were released the same week that renewed US-Iran hostilities pushed oil prices sharply higher, and the coincidence is not incidental: energy-driven inflation is precisely the kind of shock that hands the hawkish wing of the committee the evidence it needs to justify holding rates higher for longer.

- A Fed this divided is harder for markets to read than one with clear forward guidance, and the swings in rate-hike probability seen this week — jumping within a single trading day on a single presidential statement — illustrate how much more reactive to headlines the whole rates complex has become under Warsh's data-dependent, guidance-light approach.

title: France's Big Three Carve Up SFR in €20.35bn Deal, Ending the Four-Operator Era
summary: Bouygues Telecom, Orange and Iliad signed an agreement to acquire Altice France's SFR business for €20.35 billion, splitting its customers, network assets and spectrum between them rather than one buyer taking the whole company. The deal matters as a structural shift for European telecoms: after years of regulators blocking in-market consolidation to protect competition, France's largest carriers have found a way to shrink from four national operators to three, a template other saturated telecom markets are likely to watch closely.
context:
- Altice France, SFR's heavily indebted parent, had been under pressure to sell for years; a three-way carve-up split among all of its main domestic rivals only became workable once the operators agreed to divide assets rather than compete to buy the whole business, avoiding a single dominant acquirer that regulators would be more likely to block.

- Under the agreed split, Bouygues takes roughly 42% of the value including SFR's enterprise business and around 5.9 million consumer customers, Iliad takes about 31% including SFR's budget brand RED and roughly 6 million customers, and Orange takes the remaining 27% including more premium subscribers and spectrum.

- European telecom markets have spent over a decade with four-plus operators per country, a structure regulators favoured for keeping consumer prices low but which left carriers with thin margins to fund network investment, including the 5G and fibre build-outs now expected of them.

- The deal still needs regulatory approval that could take up to a year, and includes an earn-out of up to €650 million as well as potential downward price adjustments tied to SFR's financial performance before the transaction closes — terms that reflect lingering uncertainty about the target's underlying health.

- If cleared, the transaction would reduce France to three major operators and is likely to be read across the sector as a signal that consolidation-starved European telecom markets may finally have found a regulatory-friendly mechanism — splitting the target among incumbents — for achieving the scale that pure two-way mergers have repeatedly failed to secure.
